source.title: Over-parameterization as a Catalyst for Better Generalization of Deep ReLU network

record.file_problem: The supplied text is the full paper and supplementary material. Its title differs from the provided TITLE metadata: the text is “Student Specialization in Deep Rectified Networks With Finite Width and Input Dimension.”
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports its own experiments on SGD training and student specialization, including CIFAR-10 and synthetic teacher-student networks. These results bear on whether width and training conditions affect the learned outcome, but it measures specialization and loss/accuracy rather than the claim versions’ general training classification-error outcome.
record.gate_note: The paper studies supervised regression from a fixed teacher and reports specialization correlations, MSE/log loss, and evaluation accuracy. These are not direct measurements of training classification error from random initialization on CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100. CIFAR-10 is trained with cross-entropy for one experiment, but the stated results are evaluation accuracy and teacher correlation. No result tests random or corrupted labels.
record.test_reason: The study measures teacher-node specialization, regression loss and evaluation accuracy. It does not establish spurious-local-minimum frequencies or their reduction with extra width (V2), and it does not measure the outcomes or comparisons named by the other versions. Its specialization theorems assume small per-sample gradients rather than proving that training reaches them.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially correct. Under dataset, teacher-separation and observer conditions, sufficiently small per-sample gradients imply lowest-layer teacher-node specialization. The finite-sample results require specified augmentation. Experiments show stronger specialization with greater student width. These are conditional recovery results, not guarantees that SGD reaches the required gradient condition.
record.recipe_differences: Teacher-student regression with a fixed teacher, SGD and ReLU/Leaky ReLU students; experiments measure specialization and loss/accuracy rather than the claim’s classification-error outcome.
record.method_sensitivity: Student over-realization, teacher-node strength/polarity, sample count, loss (MSE versus cross-entropy), dataset construction (teacher-aware versus teacher-agnostic), and layer affect the reported specialization or losses.

fits_no_version.finding: Greater student width improves teacher-node specialization; the authors report that an equal-width student can remain stuck despite sufficient representational capacity. They do not establish that these failures are spurious local minima.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In the tested teacher-student networks, additional student width improves recovery of teacher representations.

fits_no_version.finding: Stronger teacher nodes specialize earlier and more reliably; weaker nodes can remain unrecovered after extended training.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Teacher fan-out strength affects the timing and reliability of student specialization.

fits_no_version.finding: Increasing sample counts improves specialization and generalization in deep teacher-student networks, with the lowest layer aligning best.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sample count and layer affect specialization under MSE and cross-entropy training.

fits_no_version.finding: CIFAR-10 average evaluation accuracy increases from 79.67% at 1× width to 83.09% at 2× and 83.85% at 5×, alongside stronger specialization.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Wider students improve specialization and evaluation accuracy in this CIFAR-10 teacher-student setup.

fits_no_version.finding: Teacher-aware datasets produce substantially lower evaluation MSE than teacher-agnostic datasets while training MSE is low in both.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Dataset construction affects generalization in teacher-student regression even when both training losses are low.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 37th International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 119, 2020
record.problems: The paper's empirical results primarily use plotted curves with no numerical tables or uncertainty bars. Its specialization theory concerns lowest-layer alignment under specific teacher-student assumptions; the experiments do not directly measure training classification error for the claim versions.
record.rows_left_out: No additional eligible results omitted. Several plotted metrics have no exact numerical values in the text and are recorded as figure-only.

untested.parts: Training classification error on CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100, including random or corrupted labels and size, stopping or regularization effects.

Spurious-local-minimum frequencies under gradient descent, joint teacher/student width scaling, and the effect of one or two extra student neurons. Specialization failures and qualitative reports of getting stuck do not identify these minima.
Depth-dependent training-error degradation and comparisons involving identity shortcuts, special tanh initializations or Fixup.
Initialization comparisons, signal/gradient propagation, training speed and maximum trainable depth.
Learning rates relative to stability thresholds, curvature dynamics, catapult recovery and divergence.
Batch-normalization comparisons, learning-rate tolerance and normalization-free Fixup training.

record.verdict_notes: No version-specific verdict is warranted. The qualitative equal-width training difficulty is relevant context for V2 but does not identify local minima or measure their frequency. Figure 5's rounded 0.00 losses should not be interpreted as exact interpolation or as contradicting the separate specialization difficulty.

versions.untested_parts: Near-zero training classification error on CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100, corrupted or random labels, and effects of size, stopping, or regularization are not measured.

This paper varies student over-realization in teacher-student experiments, but does not test two-layer ReLU teacher-student spurious local minima frequency as teacher and student widths grow together or the one/two-neuron excess comparison described by V2.
It does not compare plain networks of increasing depth with identity-shortcut networks, or test normalization and shortcut effects on training error.
It does not compare initialization schemes or measure initialization effects on trainable depth or training speed.
It does not study learning rates relative to a stability threshold, loss curvature, or edge-of-stability dynamics.
It does not compare batch normalization with no normalization or test Fixup.
